715.title: Jesus wept
715.hook: at his friend Lazarus's tomb, Jesus weeps (John 11:35)
715.howItsDone: Christians read John 11 in worship and in times of grief, and some point to Jesus's tears as a sign that mourning belongs inside faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: out of the depths, and a long wait for the light. Your line was more than watchmen for the morning. Did you catch the light arriving at a window? Today, from the Psalms to the Gospels, and a tomb in Bethany. Day seven hundred fifteen.

"Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." That's the whole message. Two sisters, Mary and Martha, send it to Jesus about their brother Lazarus. They don't ask for anything in so many words. They just tell him: the one you love is sick. A message like that, sent from a sickbed, hardly needs to add the word come. But by the time Jesus reaches their village, Lazarus has already been in the tomb four days.
screen: `HE WHOM THOU LOVEST IS SICK.` → `IT HARDLY NEEDS TO SAY COME.` → `FOUR DAYS IN THE TOMB.`

segments.voice: First, the same sentence, twice. Martha hears he's coming and goes out to meet him on the road. Her first words: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Later Mary comes, falls at his feet, and says the very same words: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Two sisters, one sentence. Grief can find one line and say it again. Second, he is troubled. When Jesus sees Mary weeping, and the people who came with her weeping too, John says he "groaned in the spirit, and was troubled." He asks where they've laid him. They say: come and see. Third, two words. Then comes the verse itself: "Jesus wept." No explanation. No speech about it. Just tears. And the people standing there say: "Behold how he loved him!" The tears are how they see the love. Fourth, tears before the miracle. Then there's the timing. Earlier in the same chapter, Jesus told his disciples he was going to wake Lazarus out of sleep. And a few verses after he weeps, he stands at the tomb and calls, "Lazarus, come forth." And Lazarus comes out. So in John's telling, the tears don't come instead of hope. They come right alongside it. Christians read this scene in different ways, and some readers find in it grief and hope standing at the same graveside. In the story itself, the people standing by read the tears one way: as love.
screen: `THE SAME SENTENCE, TWICE.` · `HE GROANED, AND WAS TROUBLED.` · `TWO WORDS: JESUS WEPT.` · `TEARS BEFORE THE MIRACLE.` · then, large: `JESUS WEPT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the face soften: the forehead, the eyes, the jaw. Bring to mind a loss. Maybe a person, a place, a time of life that's gone. Let it come close. If tears come, let them come. Nobody's watching, and there's nothing to fix. If they don't come, that's fine too. Just let the sadness have room in the chest, without hurrying it along or talking it down. If you pray, you can bring the loss there without asking for anything, the way the sisters only said: the one you love is sick. The bell holds the time.
Jesus wept: at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, in John's Gospel, Jesus weeps, and the people say, behold how he loved him. Today's word.
Your line: behold how he loved him. Today, if sadness comes, yours or someone else's, don't rush it out of the room. Let it stay one moment longer than you'd like. Day seven hundred fifteen.

he tells her not to cry, since Lazarus will live

fork.reveal: he groans in the spirit, asks where they laid him, and weeps, even though he is about to call Lazarus out.

trapdoor: what you thought: "Jesus wept" is mostly a famous short verse.
what it means: at his friend's tomb Jesus is troubled and weeps, and the people see in it how much he loved him.
what a scholar hears: in John 11 the tears come after Jesus says he will wake Lazarus (11:11) and just before 'Lazarus, come forth' (11:43): grief and the miracle in one scene.

716.title: Let this cup pass
716.hook: the night before his death, Jesus prays in anguish in the garden (Matthew 26:36–39)
716.carry: not as I will, but as thou wilt
716.howItsDone: Christians read the Gethsemane story especially in Holy Week, and some keep a watch of prayer on the night of Holy Thursday, remembering the request to watch with him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a tomb in Bethany, and two words that hold a whole grief. Your line was behold how he loved him. Did you let some sadness stay a moment longer than you wanted to? Today, a garden at night, and a prayer with no polish on it. Day seven hundred sixteen.

Supper is over. Matthew says they sang a hymn and went out into the mount of Olives, to a place called Gethsemane. It is night. Jesus tells his disciples to sit and wait while he goes on to pray. He takes three of them further: Peter, and the two sons of Zebedee. Then, to these closest friends, he says plainly how it is with him: "My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me." No brave face. No speech. He just asks them to stay awake with him. Today, the prayer he prays a few steps further on.
screen: `A HYMN, THEN A GARDEN AT NIGHT.` → `THREE FRIENDS TAKEN FURTHER IN.` → `EXCEEDING SORROWFUL.`

segments.voice: First, flat on his face. Matthew says he went a little further, and fell on his face. Not standing, not composed. Down on the ground. The body says it before the words do. Second, the honest ask. Here is the prayer: "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me." Some readers hear an echo of the prophets here, where a cup can stand for a hard portion someone is handed to drink. And Jesus asks, plainly, not to have to drink it. He doesn't dress the wish up as something nobler. He says what he wants. Third, both halves. The same breath goes on: "nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." The wish isn't taken back to make room for the trust, and the trust doesn't erase the wish. They sit side by side in one sentence. Christians read this line in different ways. Some see in it the full humanity of Jesus, a real will that shrinks from pain. Some see in it the shape of honest prayer: ask first, then let go. Fourth, friends asleep, and a second prayer. He comes back and finds the three asleep. "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" Then Matthew says he goes away and prays again, and then a third time, saying the same words. And the words shift. The second time, Matthew gives them as: "O my Father, if this cup may not pass away from me, except I drink it, thy will be done." The first prayer asked if it be possible. The second already sounds like a man who has heard the answer, and still calls him Father.
screen: `FLAT ON HIS FACE.` · `THE HONEST ASK.` · `BOTH HALVES IN ONE SENTENCE.` · `FRIENDS ASLEEP, A SECOND PRAYER.` · then, large: `LET THIS CUP PASS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the hands rest open on your knees. Bring to mind something hard, ahead of you or around you, that you wish were different. Don't make it noble. Look for the plain wish underneath: I wish this weren't happening. I wish it would end. Say it, silently or in a whisper, in your own ordinary words. Then simply breathe beside it. Nothing needs to come after it. If you pray, you can offer the wish just as it is, unpolished, the way it was said in the garden. The bell holds the time.
Gethsemane, the garden where Jesus prayed to let the cup pass, then added, not as I will, but as thou wilt. Today's word.
Your line: not as I will, but as thou wilt. Today, when someone asks how you are, or you ask yourself, try one honest answer about what you wish, said plainly. Day seven hundred sixteen.

trapdoor: what you thought: "let this cup pass" is an old way to wish a chore away.
what it means: in Gethsemane Jesus asks honestly to be spared, then adds: not as I will, but as thou wilt.
what a scholar hears: Matthew has the prayer said again a second and a third time (26:42, 44), and some readers hear in 'cup' the prophets' cup of a hard portion (Isaiah 51:17).

717.title: Not alone in it
717.hook: Christians see in the cross a God who suffers with humanity
717.howItsDone: Christians meditate on the cross, especially in Holy Week and on Good Friday, as the place where God shares human suffering, and visit the sick and grieving as a work of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the garden at night, and a prayer that asked for the hard thing to be taken away. Your line was not as I will, but as thou wilt. Did you say out loud, to anyone, what you honestly wished? Today, the cup is not taken. Day seven hundred seventeen.
screen: `NOT AS I WILL, BUT AS THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: The garden prayer asked for the cup to pass. In Matthew's telling, it doesn't. Within hours there is an arrest, a trial before the high priest, a night of denials, and then a place called Golgotha. Christian teaching reads the cross in more than one way. Some readings ask what it paid for, or what it won. Today's reading asks something quieter. Who is on that cross, and which side of the pain is he standing on? Watching it from above, or inside it?
screen: `THE CUP DOES NOT PASS.` → `A PLACE CALLED GOLGOTHA.` → `WHICH SIDE OF THE PAIN?`

segments.voice: First, a name. In its first chapter, Matthew's Gospel gives a child the name Emmanuel, and it translates the name for its readers: "God with us." Not God above us, or God watching us. With. Second, the cross. Christians read the crucifixion through that name. In their telling, the one hanging there is not a stranger to pain watching it from far off. He is inside it: betrayed by a friend, deserted, beaten, mocked. And near the end, Matthew records him crying out with the opening line of a psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" That's the King James wording. Even the feeling of being abandoned, in this reading, is a place he has been. Third, a letter. The Letter to the Hebrews puts it this way: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities." A double negative, almost shy. It means he can be touched. He knows what weakness feels like from the inside. Fourth, how churches say it. Christians describe Christ's suffering in different words. Some theologians speak of God himself suffering on the cross. Others hold that the divine nature cannot suffer, and that the Son suffered truly in his human nature. Both are trying to keep hold of the same thing: on the cross, Christians say, God came into the worst of human pain, not only above it. The cup is not taken away. In this reading, it is drunk by someone on the inside of suffering, so that nobody in it is alone.
screen: `EMMANUEL: GOD WITH US.` · `INSIDE THE PAIN, NOT WATCHING IT.` · `TOUCHED WITH THE FEELING.` · `CHURCHES SAY IT DIFFERENT WAYS.` · then, large: `NOT ALONE IN IT.`

segments.voice: Let the shoulders drop. Bring to mind someone who is suffering right now. A friend, a parent, a neighbor, someone in the news. You don't need to fix anything. Breathing in, say their name silently. Breathing out, say: not alone. Keep that rhythm. If the mind starts drafting advice, let the draft go and come back to the name. Near the end, choose one small way to keep them company today: a message, a call, a visit. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Emmanuel, the name Matthew gives Jesus, meaning God with us, inside suffering and not only above it. Today's word.
Your line: he can be touched. Today, keep company with one person who is going through something hard. A message, a call, a chair pulled up. No advice needed. Day seven hundred seventeen.

trapdoor: what you thought: the cross is only about something paid or settled.
what it means: Christians also see in it a God who comes into suffering, so that no one is in it alone.
what a scholar hears: Emmanuel in Matthew 1:23, the cry of Psalm 22 in Matthew 27:46, Hebrews 4:15, and an old debate over whether the divine nature can suffer.

718.title: Paul's thorn
718.hook: Paul asks three times for a "thorn in the flesh" to go, and hears: my grace is sufficient
718.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to 2 Corinthians 12 in illness or long struggle, praying for healing while also praying for grace to bear what stays.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cross, read as God on the inside of suffering. Your line was he can be touched. Who did you keep company with? Today, a man who asked for his pain to go, and was told no. Day seven hundred eighteen.

Paul of Tarsus, the traveling apostle, writes letters to young churches. He has been shipwrecked, he says, beaten, jailed. And in one letter to the church in Corinth, he admits something small and stubborn. There was a thorn. Something in his body, or his life, that hurt and wouldn't leave. He asked God to take it away. He asked again. He asked a third time. Then he tells us the answer he got. It wasn't the one he asked for.
screen: `A TRAVELING APOSTLE.` → `A THORN THAT WOULDN'T LEAVE.` → `HE ASKED THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: First, the thorn. In the King James Bible, Paul writes that "there was given to me a thorn in the flesh." He never says what it was. Some readers have guessed an illness, or trouble with his eyes, or the people who opposed him. The letter keeps its secret. And that silence leaves room: a reader can set their own thorn in its place. Second, the asking. "For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me." Three times. Paul isn't stoic about it. He wants it gone, and he says so, like the prayer in the garden two days ago. Third, the answer. "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The thorn stays. What changes is where Paul looks for strength. Not in being rid of the weakness, but somewhere inside it. Grace, in Christian teaching, is God's gift, given and not earned. Here it is a gift that comes not as a cure, but as enough. Fourth, the turn. A verse later, Paul sums it up: "for when I am weak, then am I strong." It sounds like a riddle. Some Christians read it this way: the weak place is where a person stops pretending to manage alone, and makes room for God's help, and other people's. In this reading, the thorn doesn't make Paul smaller. It makes him someone who can be helped.
screen: `A THORN HE NEVER NAMES.` · `HE ASKED THREE TIMES.` · `MY GRACE IS SUFFICIENT FOR THEE.` · `WHEN I AM WEAK, THEN AM I STRONG.` · then, large: `STRENGTH IN WEAKNESS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Name one weakness of your own. Not a dramatic one; a real one. A thing you can't do well, or can't do alone right now. Notice how you usually handle it: hide it, push through, apologize for it. Now, for these two minutes, picture one person who could help with it. See yourself asking. Notice what happens in your chest when you imagine saying yes to their help. If you pray, you can bring the weakness to God the way Paul did. The bell holds the time.
Paul's thorn: a pain Paul never names, asked away three times, and answered: my grace is sufficient for thee. Today's word.
Your line: strength in weakness. Today, accept help with one weakness, small or large, without explaining it away. Day seven hundred eighteen.

719.title: With hardship, ease
719.hook: with every hardship comes ease, said twice
719.howItsDone: Muslims may recite this chapter in prayer, and some say its line about hardship and ease to one another in difficult times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Paul's thorn, asked away three times, and still there. Your line was strength in weakness. Did you let someone help? Today the theme of suffering moves to the Quran, and a short chapter with a line said twice. Day seven hundred nineteen.

"But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease." That's Marmaduke Pickthall's English, translating two short verses of the Quran. Read it slowly and something odd happens. The second line adds nothing new. Apart from the 'but' that opens the first, it's the same words in the same order. In an essay, you'd cut it. And yet there it is, said again, the way you'd say something twice to a friend who didn't quite hear you the first time. Or didn't quite believe it. Today, the chapter those lines come from, and why the repeat matters.
screen: `WITH HARDSHIP GOETH EASE.` → `SAID AGAIN, ALMOST WORD FOR WORD.` → `WHY SAY IT TWICE?`

segments.voice: First, the chapter. It's one of the short ones near the end of the Quran, called the Expansion, or the Opening Up. Tradition says it came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at a hard time. It begins with questions: did God not open up your chest, and lift from you the burden that weighed down your back? Before any promise, it remembers relief that has already come. Second, the small word. Pickthall doesn't write after hardship. He writes with hardship. The ease isn't only waiting at the far end of the road. It walks alongside the hard thing, already present in it, even when it's hard to see. Third, the repeat. The line comes twice. Some readers hear it as emphasis, the way a person repeats what matters. Some commentators go further: they read the twice-said line as one hardship met by two eases. Either way, the chapter won't let the reassurance be said only once. Fourth, what comes after. The chapter doesn't end in comfort and a nap. Its closing verses turn to work and to God: when you're free of one task, keep at the next, and turn your longing to your Lord. Ease, in this reading, isn't escape from life. It's what makes it possible to keep going inside it.
screen: `A CHAPTER THAT REMEMBERS RELIEF.` · `WITH, NOT AFTER.` · `SAID TWICE: TWO EASES?` · `THEN, BACK TO WORK.` · then, large: `WITH HARDSHIP, EASE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one hardship you're carrying right now. Don't argue with it; just let it be there. Now look inside it, not after it, for one ease. Something small that's with you in it. A person who checks in. A warm meal. A moment when the worry went quiet. A strength you didn't know you had. When you find one, rest your attention there for a few breaths. Then the hardship, then the ease again. Both are here. The bell holds the time.
With hardship: the opening of a line the Quran says twice, with hardship goeth ease. With, not after. Today's word.
Your line: it walks alongside. Today, when something hard comes, look for one ease already inside it, and name it to yourself. Say it twice if you need to. Day seven hundred nineteen.

720.title: Patience in the Quran
720.hook: the Quran praises patient endurance and prayer
720.carry: patience is at the first stroke
720.howItsDone: Muslims speak of sabr as a virtue to practice in hardship, in daily duties and in restraint, and pair it with prayer, as the Quran does.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a line the Quran says twice. Your line was it walks alongside. What ease did you find inside something hard? Today, a word the Quran reaches for when hardship comes. Day seven hundred twenty.

A woman is weeping at a grave. A man passing by stops and tells her to fear God and be patient. She snaps at him: leave me alone, you haven't been hit by what hit me. She doesn't know who he is. Later someone tells her: that was the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. She hurries to his door to apologize, and finds no guards there, just the man. And what he says to her, in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari, is one short sentence about when patience counts. Today's word is that patience.
screen: `A WOMAN WEEPING AT A GRAVE.` → `LEAVE ME ALONE.` → `SHE HURRIES TO HIS DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Arabic it's sabr. English often says patience, but in one verse of the second chapter, Pickthall reaches for a sturdier word: "O ye who believe! Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast." Steadfastness. Not waiting quietly in a line. Standing your ground while something hard goes on. Second, the pairing. Sabr doesn't come alone in that verse. It comes with prayer. Endurance and turning to God are offered together, as help, not as a test you pass on your own strength. And the verse ends with a place to stand: God is with the steadfast. Third, the honesty. Two verses later, the Quran doesn't promise an easy life. It says plainly that people will be tried with some fear and hunger, with loss of wealth and lives and crops. Then it says: give good news to the steadfast. Sabr isn't the absence of hardship. It's what someone does in the middle of one. Fourth, back to the grave. The Prophet's answer to the woman, as al-Bukhari records it, is that patience is at the first stroke. Not weeks later, once the worst has passed. At the first blow. It isn't a ban on tears; in another hadith, the Prophet weeps at a death himself. Sabr, in this reading, is the first moment's choice of how to meet what has hit you: with tears if they come, but without turning on the person beside you, or on God.
screen: `SABR: STEADFASTNESS.` · `PATIENCE AND PRAYER, TOGETHER.` · `TRIED WITH FEAR AND LOSS.` · `PATIENCE AT THE FIRST STROKE.` · then, large: `ALLAH IS WITH THE STEADFAST.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath come and go. Think back to the last small blow you took. A sharp word. Bad news. A plan that fell through. Remember the first second of it: the jolt, the heat, what you said or nearly said. Now replay that first second slowly. Let the feeling be there, fully. And then, in the replay, take one breath before anything else happens. Just one. That breath is a patient moment. Rest in it for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Sabr: Arabic, patience, steadfastness. In the Quran it comes with prayer, and God is with the steadfast. Today's word.
Your line: patience is at the first stroke. Today, when the first blow of something lands, big or small, practice one patient moment: one breath before the first reply. Day seven hundred twenty.

trapdoor: what you thought: patience means waiting quietly for things to get better.
what it means: sabr is steadfastness in the middle of hardship, paired with prayer, and it counts most at the first blow.
what a scholar hears: sabr in Quran 2:153–157, and the hadith of the woman at the grave in Sahih al-Bukhari, 'patience is at the first stroke.'

721.title: To God we return
721.hook: Muslims say "to God we belong and to God we return" on hearing of a loss
721.carry: who could be better than him
721.howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un on hearing of a death or another loss, and write it in messages of condolence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the woman at the grave, and patience at the first stroke. Your line was patience is at the first stroke. Did you find one breath before the first reply? Today, the words the Quran puts in the mouths of the steadfast. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

The phone lights up with a message from a Muslim friend: her grandmother has died. Under it, the replies start arriving, one after another, and they begin with the same Arabic phrase, or its initials. The phrase is inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Different people, different spellings, the same sentence. Muslims say it on hearing of a death, and of other losses too. It isn't a condolence card. It's a verse. Today, where the line comes from: yesterday's passage.
screen: `A MESSAGE: HER GRANDMOTHER HAS DIED.` → `THE SAME SENTENCE, OVER AND OVER.` → `NOT A CARD. A VERSE.`

segments.voice: First, where it comes from. Yesterday's verses said people will be tried with fear and loss, and gave good news to the steadfast. The next verse describes them: they are those "Who say, when a misfortune striketh them: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." That's Pickthall's English. The patient are known by what they say. Second, two halves. We are God's: in this reading, whatever was lost was never simply owned. Not the money, not the health, not even the people we love. And unto Him we are returning: the one who has died has gone back where everyone is going. The sentence holds the loss and the hope in a single breath. Third, a widow's story. In the hadith collection of Muslim, Umm Salama tells how the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught that someone struck by a loss should say this verse, and ask God for reward in the affliction and something better in its place. When her husband Abu Salama died, she said it, and wondered who could be better than him. Later the Prophet himself asked to marry her. She said it before she could imagine any answer. Fourth, looking back. This is the end of a week on suffering. Two grieving sisters with the same sentence, and Jesus weeping with them. A wish, said plainly in a garden. The cross, read as company. A thorn that stayed. Ease, promised twice. Patience at the first stroke. And now a sentence for the moment the news arrives. Again and again this week, the texts give people words to say in the worst moment, and leave the why unanswered.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, hands in your lap. Think of something you once called yours and no longer have: a person, a home, a job, the body you had at twenty. Name it silently, by its plain name. Now try the verse's shape in your own words, if it fits for you: first, where it came from, then, where it has gone. Or simply: it was given; it is gone; it mattered. If you're Muslim, or if you wish, you can say the verse itself over it. Then let the words go quiet, and let the loss stay a while in the silence after them. The bell holds the time.
Umm Salama, the widow in the hadith who said this verse on losing her husband, and whom the Prophet later asked to marry. Today's word.
Your line: who could be better than him. Today, honor one loss in words: write it, say it to someone, or speak it quietly to yourself. Day seven hundred twenty-one.
